content.overview: BNS s. 54 — Abettor present when offence is committed.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Abettor present when offence is committed. BNS restatement of IPC 114. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 114. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 54 is the rule on “Abettor present when offence is committed”. The section provides that whenever any person, who is absent would be liable to be punished as an abettor, is present when the act or offence for which he would be punishable in consequence of the abetment is committed, he shall be deemed to have committed such act or offence. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 54 exists so that “Abettor present when offence is committed” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
54. Whenever any person, who is absent would be liable to be punished as an abettor, is present when the act or offence for which he would be punishable in consequence of the abetment is committed, he shall be deemed to have committed such act or offence
